summary: The article examines the digital divide in local schools, where students lacking devices or reliable internet fall behind as curricula go digital. It covers causes (income, geography, infrastructure), local testimonies, and community responses since September 2023, including Digital Bridge, school policy changes, corporate and philanthropic support, and calls for systemic policy. It stresses that training and community involvement are essential alongside distributing technology.
one_line: Local article on how the digital divide hurts students and how community groups, schools, companies, and policymakers are responding since September 2023.
key_facts: A survey by the article's team in October 2023 found 30% of students in the area had difficulty completing assignments due to unreliable internet or insufficient devices at home.
Digital Bridge, a community-led initiative founded by tech entrepreneur Michael Smith in November 2023, offers devices plus maintenance, software, and training for students and educators.
Digital Bridge has supplied over 200 devices to students in need and partnered with a local internet service provider for discounted rates for low-income families.
Samantha Green, principal at Westview High School, revised school policies to support students without reliable digital access.
Westview High School rolled out a 'tech-buddy' system, extended computer lab hours, and offers a checkout system for laptops and hotspots.
A town hall meeting on January 15, 2024 featured heated discussions among community members, educators, and representatives; activist James Carter called for comprehensive local and state policy.
Policymaker Ellen Thompson said options under consideration include tax incentives for tech donations and greater investment in public Wi-Fi hotspots.
Helios Electronics started the 'Tech for Tomorrow' initiative, which since February 2024 has worked with school districts on donations and educational programs.
The Clarkson Foundation granted $500,000 in March 2024 for technology for low-income students; president Linda Clark called it a 'moral obligation'.
The local community college has offered free digital literacy workshops since April 2024 for adults and children.
Causes of the divide include socioeconomic status, geographic location, and local infrastructure; rural providers often lack return on investment to expand service.
Eighth-grader Ricardo Martinez said his family, with a mother working two jobs, couldn't afford Wi-Fi until recently and he fell behind on projects.
